 Social Security’s 3.6% raise could trigger a tax on your benefits: the $25,000 line that never moves
 08/11/2026 10:35 by Francisco Zuasti 
 Next year’s 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) will put more money in the pockets of nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries, according to the Social Security Administration (SSA). For some retirees, it could also nudge them across an income line that decides whether the IRS can tax part of those benefits.
 That line has one unusual feature: unlike the COLA itself, it does not rise with inflation. As the IRS updates the 2027 brackets and the deductions for people over 65 , here is how the math works and how to tell whether your raise matters at tax time.
 Where exactly is the line?
 The IRS looks at what it calls combined income. You take half of your Social Security benefits and add all your other income, including pensions, wages, interest, dividends and tax-exempt interest.
 According to IRS Publication 915 , then you compare that total with these limits:
 Single filers: below $25,000, none of your benefits are taxable. Between $25,000 and $34,000, up to 50% can be. Above $34,000, up to 85% can be.
 Married couples filing jointly: below $32,000, none of your benefits are taxable. Between $32,000 and $44,000, up to 50% can be. Above $44,000, up to 85% can be.
 Those percentages describe how much of your benefit can count as taxable income, not the tax rate. Nobody pays 85% of their Social Security to the IRS.
 How can a raise push you over?
 Picture a single retiree who receives $2,000 a month and has $13,000 a year from a small pension. In 2026, half of the benefits ($12,000) plus the pension comes to exactly $25,000, right at the limit.
 With a 3.6% raise, the monthly benefit climbs to $2,072, or $24,864 for the year. Half of that plus the same pension is $25,432. That retiree is now $432 over the line, even though nothing else has changed.
 The practical effect is small here. Only about $216 of benefits would become taxable income, and with the standard deduction this person probably still owes no federal income tax. The point is that the limit is fixed while benefits keep growing, so more retirees cross it every year.
 Who should pay the most attention?
 The raise matters more for people who already have other income. Take a couple filing jointly with $48,000 in benefits and $30,000 from pensions and investments. Their combined income is $54,000 this year and $54,864 in 2027, assuming their other income doesn’t change.
 Because they are above $44,000, the worksheet in Publication 915 adds roughly $734 to their taxable income. At a 12% rate, that works out to about $88 more in federal tax for the year. It won’t erase the raise, but it does trim it.
 Remember, too, that 2027 benefits are reported on the return you file in 2028. A few states also tax Social Security under their own rules, so it pays to check where you live.
 What can you do about it?
 You can’t change the limits, but you can avoid a surprise at tax time:
 Add up your expected 2027 income once you know your new benefit. The SSA says COLA notices will reach most beneficiaries online in late November, in the Message Center of your my Social Security account .
 Watch the timing of IRA withdrawals and investment sales, since they count toward combined income.
 Ask the SSA to withhold federal tax from your check by filing Form W-4V if you’d rather not make a lump-sum payment. The SSA explains the process on its benefits and taxes page .
 If your situation is more complicated, a tax professional or an IRS-sponsored volunteer site can run the numbers with you before you file.
